report.title: ANVAYA report · DEMO · Indian smartphone market

blocks.text: Across 140 simulated agents and 24 rounds, final mean opinion was -0.05 (support 46, neutral 57, oppose 37); polarisation index 0.54; 5 communities formed.

Scenario assumption at round 9 (“A rival brand announces a 20% price cut on its comparable flagship — Scripted scenario ass”) moved mean opinion by -0.08 within three rounds. This effect size is an unverified assumption.
Prioritise engagement with the 'Price-sensitive families' segment, which ends least favourable (mean -0.85).
Engage high-influence voices such as profiles like 'Sana Khan' (Tech enthusiasts).
Synthetic demonstration: a flagship smartphone launches in India; at round 9 a rival announces a 20% price cut (scripted).
Show how opinion forms, spreads and shifts in a simulated society.

Methodology: Multi-agent simulation of interacting individuals; Diagnostic analysis of what drove changes in a run; Scenario analysis (baseline vs alternative assumptions); One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis of the key assumption; Monte Carlo replicates of the stochastic simulation model. The question concerns how many interacting people form, spread or change opinions — an emergent social process that aggregate statistics cannot represent, so a multi-agent simulation is warranted. The question compares alternative assumptions, so scenario and sensitivity analysis are used. The simulation is stochastic, so results are reported across replicates with intervals instead of single runs.
No documents were supplied; the population and scenarios rest on simulation assumptions only.
Simulated segment “Students” (n=30): mean opinion -0.08 → -0.06.
Simulated segment “Young professionals” (n=28): mean opinion +0.09 → -0.02.
Simulated segment “Brand loyalists” (n=20): mean opinion +0.48 → +0.51.
Simulated segment “Price-sensitive families” (n=31): mean opinion -0.70 → -0.85.
Simulated segment “Tech enthusiasts” (n=20): mean opinion +0.65 → +0.60.
Simulated segment “Value-seeking switchers” (n=11): mean opinion +0.03 → -0.04.
No knowledge graph was built for this project.
140 agents across 6 segments: Students (22%); Young professionals (20%); Tech enthusiasts (14%); Price-sensitive families (22%); Brand loyalists (14%); Value-seeking switchers (8%).
Assumption: Segment shares, trait distributions, names and opinions are illustrative simulation assumptions — not survey data.
Assumption: The competitor price cut in round 9 is a scripted what-if, not a forecast.
Population basis: demo. Attributes not stated in supplied evidence are simulation assumptions. All agents are fictional; none represent real individuals.
Recorded interactions: 344 post, 404 reply, 80 disagree, 361 agree, 258 share. Disagreement rate among agree/disagree responses: 18%.

Most influential agent profiles (PageRank on who changed whose opinion): Sana Khan (Tech enthusiasts, 1.00); Nisha Nair (Tech enthusiasts, 0.80); Dev Menon (Young professionals, 0.69); Diya Gill (Tech enthusiasts, 0.60); Priya Bose (Tech enthusiasts, 0.59).
Mean opinion moved +0.01 → -0.05; polarisation 0.52 → 0.54; communities 5 → 5.

Across 12 Monte Carlo replicates, final mean opinion averaged +0.04 (5–95%: +0.01 to +0.05). Replicate-level support majority occurred 12/12 times (Beta posterior mean 0.93, 95% interval 0.75–1.00) — a model-conditional figure, not a real-world probability.
Simulation outputs are model results under stated assumptions, not predictions of what will happen.

Uncertainty: These are conditional on the model and on unverified assumptions about agents and effects. They show direction and rough size of change within the simulated society, not probabilities about the real world.
Risk: polarisation index 0.54 suggests entrenched camps.
Risk: segment “Price-sensitive families” ends least favourable (mean -0.85).
Opportunity: segment “Tech enthusiasts” ends most favourable (mean +0.60) and can be mobilised.
Opportunity: profiles like “Sana Khan” carry high influence in the simulated network.
1. Prioritise engagement with the 'Price-sensitive families' segment, which ends least favourable (mean -0.85).  [priority 63.7/100 · impact 4 feasibility 3 urgency 3 risk 2]
Reasoning: It is the segment with the lowest final mean opinion in the simulation.
Simulation findings: Price-sensitive families: mean opinion -0.70 → -0.85
Benefits: Targets the largest gap in support.
Risks: Segment attributes are simulation assumptions.
Tradeoffs: Effort diverted from already-favourable segments.
Assumptions: Segment composition reflects the real audience.
Resources: Segment-specific messaging and channel plan.
Success indicators: Segment support share rises in follow-up measurement.
2. Engage high-influence voices such as profiles like 'Sana Khan' (Tech enthusiasts).  [priority 58.8/100 · impact 4 feasibility 3 urgency 3 risk 3]
Reasoning: Highest computed influence score (PageRank on who-changed-whose-opinion).
Simulation findings: influence score 1.0
Benefits: Information cascades start from influential agents.
Risks: Real influencers may differ from simulated ones.
Tradeoffs: Dependence on few voices.
Assumptions: Influence structure resembles the simulated network.
Resources: Partnership budget
Success indicators: Cascade size, reach.
Agents are fictional. Their traits, goals and starting opinions are simulation assumptions unless a source states otherwise.
Interaction structure comes from an inspectable opinion-dynamics model (bounded confidence with backlash); language is added by deterministic templates.
Simulation results depend on the seed, population and scenario effect sizes; use the Monte Carlo intervals, not single runs.
Simulation outputs are model results under stated assumptions, not predictions of what will happen.
Single-topic opinion model: richer attitudes, offline events and media effects are not represented.
